title: Put a pH electrode away in its storage solution, not in DI water
context: Chemical technicians and lab technicians (O*NET 19-4031.00, Chemical Technicians) measure pH many times a day. Electrode makers' manuals give the same routine after a measurement: rinse the electrode in deionized (DI) water, then store it with its glass bulb and junction wet in storage solution, usually 3 M KCl. Leaving it in DI water leaches ions out of the glass membrane and the reference junction. Leaving it dry dehydrates the membrane. Either way the electrode becomes slow and drifts, and a dried or leached one may need hours of reconditioning or replacing. The beaker of DI water is the tempting place to leave it, because it is right there and looks clean. The instruction doesn't say where it goes.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A fixed electrode stand has a dark base (10 x 12 x 1.2 cm) centered at x 39, y -8, a steel rod 18 cm tall at x 38, y -8, and an arm reaching to a ring at x 27, y -8 whose top is 9 cm up, with a 2.2 cm opening. The pH electrode hangs in that ring: a black head 2.8 cm across and 3 cm tall with a silver screw connector on top (its cable unplugged), and a clear glass shaft 1.2 cm across and 8 cm long below it, with white filling, a silver wire, a white ceramic junction 1.5 cm above the tip and a round glass bulb at the tip. It weighs 40 g. Its bulb sits in a fixed 100 mL glass beaker (5 cm across, 6.8 cm tall) under the ring, holding pale yellow sample to 4.5 cm. A fixed 150 mL glass beaker of DI water (5.8 cm across, 8 cm tall, water to 5.5 cm) is at x 22, y -20, with a fixed white squeeze wash bottle with a blue cap at x 38, y -29. The storage bottle is fixed at x 30, y -22: a white plastic wide-mouth bottle 5.6 cm across, with a green and white label, clear storage solution to 6 cm and a white cap whose top is 9 cm up, with a 2.2 cm hole ringed by a black rubber grommet. The electrode is stored by lowering it through that hole until its head rests on the cap.
scoring: The electrode's tip counts as wet in a vessel when it is inside the vessel's wall, at least 2 cm below that liquid's surface (so the bulb and the junction are both covered), and the electrode is within 15 degrees of upright. It counts as stored when it is wet in the storage bottle, its head is within 1 cm of resting on the cap, and it is still. It counts as rinsed if it was wet in the DI water for at least 0.5 s at some point. The score is 0 if the electrode ever tipped more than 45 degrees for 2 control steps in a row (0.1 s at 20 Hz), as a dropped glass electrode does. Otherwise, at the end, it is 1.0 if the electrode is stored and was rinsed, 0.5 if it is stored without a rinse, and 0 if it is anywhere else, including still in the sample, left in the DI water or lying dry. The possible scores are 0, 0.5 and 1.0. In a real trial, watch the video for a dip in the DI water and for a drop, then check at the end that the electrode hangs in the storage bottle's cap.
reset_notes: Hang the electrode back in the stand's ring over the sample. Nothing is used up. In a real trial, a dummy electrode can stand in for a working one.
fidelity: Real size, except the electrode's shaft is 8 cm, shorter than the usual 12 cm, so the arm can lift it clear of the vessels. The liquids are see-through shapes that are seen but not felt, and nothing pours or drips. Round vessels collide as eight-sided walls, and the cap and ring holes as square openings. The props are modeled shapes on simple box and cylinder colliders. The simulation uses rigid-body physics only.
